Just think about how a subsidy affects the basic economics: it raises demand. You can look at it either as more people being able to attend, or as the same people who would attend being willing to pay more (e.g. whatever they were willing to pay before, plus now the subsidy.). When demand goes up, prices go up. Eventually new supply might enter the market and prices return to a point constrained by the cost of service, but university supply is slower to respond than demand (hard to start a new university, and existing universities are relatively happy to sit on the new subsidy-driven profits rather than expanding.)

We see this in healthcare too. We want to give everyone all the services they need, but the new demand for those services makes the price go up, and so we keep increasing the subsidies to keep up, but never actually can catch up unless we address the underlying problem of needing to increase the supply rather than increasing demand.
